'''William Spence''' (born 31 July 1777 in [[Greenock, Scotland|Greenock]], Scotland – died 22 May 1815 in [[Glasgow, Scotland|Glasgow]], Scotland) was a Scottish mathematician who published works on the fields of [[logarithmic functions]], [[algebraic equation]]s and their relation to [[Integral calculus|integral]] and [[differential calculus]] respectively.

== Early life, family, and personal life ==

Spence was the second son to Ninian Spence and his wife Sarah Townsend. Ninian Spence ran a [[coppersmith]] business, and the Spence family were a prominent family in [[Greenock]] at the time.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Craik |first1=Alex D.D. |title=Polylogarithms, functional equations and more: The elusive essays of William Spence (1777–1815) |journal=Historia Mathematica |date=October 2013 |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=386–422 |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2013.06.002 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Greenock - Towns - Scottish Directories - National Library of Scotland |url=https://digital.nls.uk/directories/browse/archive/87160793 |access-date=2022-06-24 |website=digital.nls.uk}}</ref>

From an early age, Spence was characterised as having a docile and reasonable nature, with him being mature for his age.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |id={{ProQuest|4520067}} |last1=Galt |first1=J. |title=THE LATE MR. WILLIAM SPENCE |journal=The Monthly Magazine |volume=47 |issue=325 |date=May 1819 |pages=373–375 }}</ref> At school he formed a life-long friendship with [[John Galt (novelist)|John Galt]], who documented much of his life and his works posthumously.<ref name=":0"/> Despite having received a formal education until he was a teenager, Spence never attended university, instead he moved to [[Glasgow]] where he lodged with a friend of his fathers, learning the skills of a manufacturer.<ref name=":0" />

Two years after his father's death in 1795, Spence returned to [[Greenock]] in 1797.<ref name=":0" /> With the support of Galt and others, he established a small [[literary society]], wherein once a month they read a range of essays on varying subjects, this society met frequently until 1804.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Galt |first=John |url=https://www.canadiana.ca/view/oocihm.37703 |title=The autobiography of John Galt |publisher=Key & Biddle |year=1833}}</ref> After this, Spence visited many places in England, he lived in London for a few months where, in 1809, he published his first work.<ref name=":0" /> In 1814, he published his second work, getting married in the same year – Spence intended to live in London, and began his journey back before becoming ill, having travelled as far as [[Glasgow]], he died in his sleep due to illness.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" />

Spence held an interest in [[musical composition]], and played the flute.<ref name=":1"/>

== Published works ==
Spence published ''An Essay on the Theory of the Various Orders of Logarithmic Transcendents: With an Inquiry Into Their Applications to the Integral Calculus and the Summation of Series in 1809.''<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Spence |first=William |oclc=10156665 |title=An Essay on the Theory of the Various Orders of Logarithmic Transcendents: With an Inquiry Into Their Applications to the Integral Calculus and the Summation of Series |date=1809 |publisher=John Murray and Archibald Constable and Company }}</ref> Throughout his work, he displayed a familiarity with the work of [[Lagrange]] and [[Louis François Antoine Arbogast|Arbogast]], which is notable since at the time very few were familiar with their works.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /> In his preface he derived the [[binomial theorem]] and mainly focused on the properties and analytic applications of the series:<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=William Spence – Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Spence/ |access-date=2022-06-24 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>\pm x/1^n - x^2/2^n \pm x^3/3^n - ...</math>

which he denoted with <math>L_n(1\pm x)</math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> He went on further to derive nine general properties of this function in a table.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

Spence goes on to calculate the values of:

:<math>L_2(x) = -\int^x_0\frac{\ln (1-t)}{t} \operatorname{d}\!t</math>

(the [[dilogarithm]]) to nine decimal places, in a table, for all [[integer]] values of <math>1 + x</math> from 1 to 100, the first ever of its kind.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> These functions became known as the [[polylogarithm]] functions, with this particular case often called [[Spence's function]] after Spence.

[[File:Spence dilogarithm table.gif|center|thumb|Spence's numerical calculation of the dilogarithm from (Spence, 1809, p. 24)]]
Later on he also created a similar table for <math>\tan^{-1}x</math>.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

Spence published his last work, ''Outlines of a theory of Algebraical Equations, deduced from the principles of Harriott, and extended to the fluxional or differential calculus was published in 1814.''<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Spence |first=William |oclc=1063204490 |title=Outlines of a theory of Algebraical Equations, deduced from the principles of Harriott, and extended to the fluxional or differential calculus |date=1814 }}</ref> In which he took a systematic approach to solving equations up to the fourth degree using symmetrical functions of the roots.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

After Spence's death, [[John Herschel]] edited ''Mathematical Essays by the late William Spence'', which was published in 1819, with John Galt writing a biography on Spence.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Spence |first=William |oclc=1021878949 |title=Mathematical Essays, by the Late William Spence, Esq. Edited by John F. W. Herschel, Esq. With a Biographical Sketch of the Author |date=1819 |publisher=Thomas and George Underwood, 32, Fleet Street }}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Spence's work was noted to be remarkable at the time, with John Herschel, his acquaintance and one of Britain's leading mathematicians at the time, had referenced it in one of his later publications ''Consideration of various points of analysis,'' which prompted [[John Herschel|Herschel]] to edit Spence's manuscripts.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal |title=XXII. Consideration of various points of analysis |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |date=31 December 1814 |volume=104 |pages=440–468 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1814.0023 |s2cid=111328500 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Spence was held in such high regard by Galt, and later Herschel that they published a collection of his individual essays in 1819.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=John Herschel Correspondence |url=http://historydb.adlerplanetarium.org/herschel/?terms=John+Galt&fields=tofrom&fields=summary&fields=location&fields=metadata&tofrom=To+JH&tofrom=From+JH&date1=1799&date2=1875&undated=on&isadvanced=false |access-date=2022-06-28 |website=historydb.adlerplanetarium.org}}</ref> Posthumously, his work was met with appreciation from his contemporaries, with a review in the ninety-fourth number of the [[Quarterly Review]] (reproduced in Galt's ''The Literary and Miscellanies of John Galt, Volume 1)'' that described his first work in 1809 as:

''" [The] first formal essay in our language on any distinct and considerable branch of the integral calculus, which has appeared since… Hellinsʼs papers on the ‘Rectification of the Conic Sections".''<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Galt |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6pEEAAAAYAAJ&q=first+formal+essay&pg=PA1 |title=The Literary Life and Miscellanies of John Galt |date=1834 |publisher=W. Blackwood |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=XVIL. Of the rectification of the conic sections |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |date=31 December 1802 |volume=92 |pages=448–476 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1802.0020 |s2cid=110222385 }}</ref>
